newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Nobel laureate urges U.S. to mediate in E.Timor.
newsitem.headline: Nobel laureate urges U.S. to mediate in E.Timor.

text.p: Nobel peace laureate Jose Ramos-Horta on Wednesday urged the United States to mediate for self-determination in East Timor which he said was a simpler problem than Bosnia or the Middle East.
Ramos-Horta said during a trip to Lisbon that the United States had made great strides for peace in Bosnia and the Middle East by overcoming differences among several parties.

"Why not in East Timor? The issue in East Timor is clear. It is an issue of decolonisation, an issue of self-determination. It involves two parties. One is the people of East Timor, the other is the republic of Indonesia," he said.
"It is a clearly defined conflict," he told a lunch of a U.S.-Portuguese friendship society.

Ramos-Horta and the Bishop of Timor Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo received the 1996 Nobel peace prize for their work to find a peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor which has been in turmoil since Indonesia annexed the tiny territory in 1976.
"We are not asking the United States or any industrialised country to impose sanctions on Indonesia," Ramos-Horta said.
He said he wanted Indonesia to withdraw from East Timor with dignity.

"We are prepared to bend backwards, to be flexible, to provide Indonesia with a way out that would first and foremost preserve the honour and dignity of the republic and the national interests of the republic of Indonesia," he said.

"The excessive military presence (of Indonesian armed forces) must be reduced drastically, human rights violations must be stopped, torture must end, trans-migration must stop, and the United Nations should establish in Dili a human rights monitoring office," the former journalist said.
Ramos-Horta said he was not optimistic that the East Timorese would win self-determination soon.
"Whoever comes after (Indonesian President) Suharto will have a better chance to resolve the problem of East Timor," he said.
"There is a growing democracy movement in Indonesia with millions of people demanding changes," he added.
"This is a time for the United States to intervene discreetly but in a sustained manner to encourage a peaceful transition in Indonesia (after Suharto)," Ramos-Horta said.
